questions.problem:
Find the Laplace transform $Y(s)=L{y(t)}$ for $s>2$ if 

$$
{y}^{′}-2y=5-2{e}^{-t},\,y(0)=\frac{1}{3}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the addition and scalar multiplication properties of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{′}-2y} & =L{5-2{e}^{-t}} \\ L{{y}^{′}}-2L{y} & =5L{1}-2L{{e}^{-t}}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate $L{{y}^{′}},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of a derivative and the initial condition $y(0)=\frac{1}{3}:$

$$
L{{y}^{′}}=sY(s)-y(0)=sY(s)-\frac{1}{3}
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{n}} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}},\,s>0,\,n\in {N}_{0} \\ L{{e}^{at}} & =\frac{1}{s-a},\,s>a\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following results:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{1} & =\frac{1}{s} \\ L{{e}^{-t}} & =\frac{1}{s-(-1)}=\frac{1}{s+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{′}}-2L{y} & =5L{1}-2L{{e}^{-t}} \\ (sY(s)-\frac{1}{3})-2Y(s) & =\frac{5}{s}-\frac{2}{s+1} \\ (s-2)Y(s) & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{5}{s}-\frac{2}{s+1} \\ (s-2)Y(s) & =\frac{s(s+1)+15(s+1)-6s}{3s(s+1)} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{{s}^{2}+10s+15}{3s(s+1)(s-2)}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the Laplace transform $Y(s)=L{y(t)}$ for $s>2$ if 

$$
{y}^{′}-2y=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y(0)=1.
$$

You may make use of the following result:

$$
L{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,s>0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the addition and scalar multiplication properties of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{′}-2y} & =L{-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\ L{{y}^{′}}-2L{y} & =-5L{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate $L{{y}^{′}},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of a derivative and the initial condition $y(0)=1:$

$$
L{{y}^{′}}=sL{y}-y(0)=sY(s)-1
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms, we have the following result:

$$
L{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}=\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1},\,s>0
$$

Therefore, we can solve for $Y(s):$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{′}}-2L{y} & =-5L{\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\ (sY(s)-1)-2Y(s) & =-5(\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1}) \\ sY(s)-2Y(s) & =1-\frac{5}{{s}^{2}+1} \\ (s-2)Y(s) & =\frac{{s}^{2}-4}{{s}^{2}+1} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{{s}^{2}-4}{({s}^{2}+1)(s-2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $s>2,$ we simplify as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Y(s) & =\frac{(s-2)(s+2)}{({s}^{2}+1)(s-2)} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{s+2}{{s}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the Laplace transform $Y(s)=L{y(t)}$ for $s>0$ if

$$
2{y}^{′}+2y=4+{t}^{2},\,y(0)=0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the addition and scalar multiplication properties of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{2{y}^{′}+2y} & =L{4+{t}^{2}} \\ 2L{{y}^{′}}+2L{y} & =4L{1}+L{{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate $L{{y}^{′}},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of a derivative and the initial condition $y(0)=0:$

$$
L{{y}^{′}}=sY(s)-y(0)=sY(s)
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms:

$$
L{{t}^{n}}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}},\,s>0,\,n\in {N}_{0}
$$

Therefore, we have the following results:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{1} & =\frac{1}{s} \\ L{{t}^{2}} & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2L{{y}^{′}}+2L{y} & =4L{1}+L{{t}^{2}} \\ 2sY(s)+2Y(s) & =4\cdot \frac{1}{s}+\frac{2}{{s}^{3}} \\ (2s+2)Y(s) & =\frac{4{s}^{2}+2}{{s}^{3}} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{2(2{s}^{2}+1)}{{s}^{3}(2s+2)} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{2{s}^{2}+1}{{s}^{3}(s+1)}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the Laplace transform $Y(s)=L{y(t)}$ for $s>3$ if 

$$
{y}^{′}+y=-8\operatorname{cosh}⁡3t,\,y(0)=1.
$$

You may make use of the following result:

$$
L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡\omega t}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}},\,s>|\omega |.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the addition and scalar multiplication properties of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{′}+y} & =L{-8\operatorname{cosh}⁡3t} \\ L{{y}^{′}}+L{y} & =-8L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡3t}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate $L{{y}^{′}},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of a derivative and the initial condition $y(0)=1:$

$$
L{{y}^{′}}=sL{y}-y(0)=sY(s)-1
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms, we have the following result:

$$
L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡3t}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-9},\,s>3
$$

Therefore, we can solve for $Y(s):$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{′}}+L{y} & =-8L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡3t} \\ (sY(s)-1)+Y(s) & =-8(\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-9}) \\ sY(s)+Y(s) & =1-\frac{8s}{{s}^{2}-9} \\ (s+1)Y(s) & =\frac{{s}^{2}-8s-9}{{s}^{2}-9} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{{s}^{2}-8s-9}{({s}^{2}-9)(s+1)}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $s>3,$ we simplify as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Y(s) & =\frac{({s}^{2}-8s-9)}{({s}^{2}-9)(s+1)} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{(s-9)(s+1)}{({s}^{2}-9)(s+1)} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{s-9}{{s}^{2}-9}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{y}^{′}+4y=2+t,\,y(0)=3.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the addition and scalar multiplication properties of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{′}+4y} & =L{2+t} \\ L{{y}^{′}}+4L{y} & =2L{1}+L{t}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate $L{{y}^{′}},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of a derivative and the initial condition $y(0)=3:$

$$
L{{y}^{′}}=sY(s)-y(0)=sY(s)-3
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms:

$$
L{{t}^{n}}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}},\,s>0,\,n\in {N}_{0}
$$

Therefore, we have the following results:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{1} & =\frac{1}{s} \\ L{t} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{′}}+4L{y} & =2L{1}+L{t} \\ (sY(s)-3)+4Y(s) & =2\cdot \frac{1}{s}+\frac{1}{{s}^{2}} \\ sY(s)+4Y(s) & =3+\frac{2}{s}+\frac{1}{{s}^{2}} \\ (s+4)Y(s) & =\frac{3{s}^{2}+2s+1}{{s}^{2}} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{3{s}^{2}+2s+1}{{s}^{2}(s+4)}\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+5y=9{e}^{3t},\,y(0)=0
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below to find the solution using Laplace transforms.

Let $Y(s)=L{y(t)}.$ Taking the Laplace transform of both sides of the equation and solving for $Y,$ we have

$$
Y(s)={{field-1}}.
$$

The partial fraction decomposition of $Y$ is

$$
Y(s)={{field-2}}.
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(t)={{field-3}}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides of the differential equation. Using the linearity property, we have

$$
L{{y}^{′}}+5L{y}=L{9{e}^{3t}}.
$$

Using the formula for the transform of a derivative, $L{{y}^{′}}=sY(s)-y(0),$ and the standard transform 

$$
L{{e}^{at}}=\frac{1}{s-a},\,s>a,
$$

 
we substitute the known values.

$$
\begin{aligned}sY(s)-0+5Y(s) & =9\cdot \frac{1}{s-3} \\ (s+5)Y(s) & =\frac{9}{s-3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for $Y(s),$ we have

$$
Y(s)=\frac{9}{(s-3)(s+5)}.
$$

Next, we perform a partial fraction decomposition. We write $Y(s)$ in the form

$$
\frac{9}{(s-3)(s+5)}=\frac{A}{s-3}+\frac{B}{s+5}.
$$

To find the constants $A$ and $B,$ we first clear the denominators:

$$
9=A(s+5)+B(s-3)
$$

Now, we find the constants $A$ and $B.$

- Setting $s=3,$ we have

$$
9=A(3+5)+B(0)\,⟹\,9=8A\,⟹\,A=\frac{9}{8}.
$$

- Setting $s=-5,$ we have

$$
9=A(0)+B(-5-3)\,⟹\,9=-8B\,⟹\,B=-\frac{9}{8}.
$$

Thus, the decomposition is

$$
Y(s)=\frac{9}{8(s-3)}-\frac{9}{8(s+5)}.
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s-3}} & ={e}^{3t} \\ {L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+5}} & ={e}^{-5t}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking the inverse Laplace transform of $Y(s),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =\frac{9}{8}{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s-3}}-\frac{9}{8}{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+5}} \\ y(t) & =\frac{9}{8}{e}^{3t}-\frac{9}{8}{e}^{-5t}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

 
we substitute the known values.

$$
\begin{aligned}sY(s)-0+3Y(s) & =4\cdot \frac{1}{s-1} \\ (s+3)Y(s) & =\frac{4}{s-1}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$
4=A(s+3)+B(s-1)

$$
4=A(1+3)+B(0)\,⟹\,4=4A\,⟹\,A=1.
$$

- Setting $s=-3,$ we have

$$
4=A(0)+B(-3-1)\,⟹\,4=-4B\,⟹\,B=-1.

$$
Y(s)=\frac{1}{s-1}-\frac{1}{s+3}.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+y=2t+4,\,y(0)=0
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below to find the solution using Laplace transforms. You may make use of the following result:

$$
L{{t}^{n}}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}},\,s>0,\,n\in {N}_{0}
$$

Let $Y(s)=L{y(t)}.$ Taking the Laplace transform of both sides of the equation and solving for $Y,$ we have

$$
Y(s)={{field-1}}.
$$

The partial fraction decomposition of $Y$ is

$$
Y(s)={{field-2}}.
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(t)={{field-3}}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides of the differential equation. Using the linearity property, we have

$$
L{{y}^{′}}+L{y}=2L{t}+4L{1}.
$$

Using the formula for the transform of a derivative $L{{y}^{′}}=sY(s)-y(0)$ and the standard polynomial transforms

$$
\begin{aligned}L{t} & =\frac{1!}{{s}^{1+1}}=\frac{1}{{s}^{2}}, \\ L{1} & =\frac{0!}{{s}^{0+1}}=\frac{1}{s},\end{aligned}
$$

we substitute the known values. Note that $y(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(sY(s)-0)+Y(s) & =2\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}}+4\cdot \frac{1}{s} \\ (s+1)Y(s) & =\frac{2}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{4}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

We rearrange to solve for $Y(s).$ First, find a common denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}(s+1)Y(s) & =\frac{2}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{4s}{{s}^{2}} \\ (s+1)Y(s) & =\frac{4s+2}{{s}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing by $(s+1),$ we obtain

$$
Y(s)=\frac{4s+2}{{s}^{2}(s+1)}.
$$

Next, we perform a partial fraction decomposition. Since the denominator has a linear factor $(s+1)$ and a repeated linear factor ${s}^{2},$ we write

$$
\frac{4s+2}{{s}^{2}(s+1)}=\frac{A}{s}+\frac{B}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{C}{s+1}.
$$

To find the constants, we clear the denominators:

$$
4s+2=As(s+1)+B(s+1)+C{s}^{2}
$$

- Setting $s=-1,$ we have
 

$$
4(-1)+2=A(0)+B(0)+C(-1)^{2}\,⟹\,-2=C\,⟹\,C=-2.
$$

- Setting $s=0,$ we have
  

$$
4(0)+2=A(0)+B(0+1)+C(0)\,⟹\,2=B\,⟹\,B=2.
$$

- Comparing the coefficients of $s,$ we have
 

$$
4=A+B\,⟹\,4=A+2\,⟹\,A=2.
$$

Thus, the decomposition is

$$
Y(s)=\frac{2}{s}+\frac{2}{{s}^{2}}-\frac{2}{s+1}.
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s}} & =1 \\ {L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{{s}^{2}}} & =t \\ {L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+1}} & ={e}^{-t}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking the inverse Laplace transform of $Y(s),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =2{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s}}+2{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{{s}^{2}}}-2{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+1}} \\ y(t) & =2+2t-2{e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+3y=4{e}^{-2t},\,y(0)=2
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below to find the solution using Laplace transforms.

Let $Y(s)=L{y(t)}.$ Taking the Laplace transform of both sides of the equation and solving for $Y,$ we have

$$
Y(s)={{field-1}}.
$$

The partial fraction decomposition of $Y$ is

$$
Y(s)={{field-2}}.
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(t)={{field-3}}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides of the differential equation. Using the linearity property, we have

$$
L{{y}^{′}}+3L{y}=L{4{e}^{-2t}}.
$$

Using the formula for the transform of a derivative, $L{{y}^{′}}=sY(s)-y(0),$ and the standard transform 

$$
L{{e}^{at}}=\frac{1}{s-a},\,s>a,
$$

we substitute the known values. Note that $y(0)=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(sY(s)-2)+3Y(s) & =4\cdot \frac{1}{s+2} \\ (s+3)Y(s)-2 & =\frac{4}{s+2}\end{aligned}
$$

We rearrange to solve for $Y(s).$ First, add $2$ to the right-hand side and find a common denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}(s+3)Y(s) & =2+\frac{4}{s+2} \\ (s+3)Y(s) & =\frac{2(s+2)}{s+2}+\frac{4}{s+2} \\ (s+3)Y(s) & =\frac{2s+8}{s+2}\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing by $(s+3),$ we obtain

$$
Y(s)=\frac{2s+8}{(s+3)(s+2)}.
$$

Next, we perform a partial fraction decomposition. We write $Y(s)$ in the form

$$
\frac{2s+8}{(s+3)(s+2)}=\frac{A}{s+3}+\frac{B}{s+2}.
$$

To find the constants $A$ and $B,$ we first clear the denominators:

$$
2s+8=A(s+2)+B(s+3)
$$

Now, we find the constants $A$ and $B.$

- Setting $s=-3,$ we have

$$
2(-3)+8=A(-3+2)+B(0)\,⟹\,2=-1A\,⟹\,A=-2.
$$

- Setting $s=-2,$ we have

$$
2(-2)+8=A(0)+B(-2+3)\,⟹\,4=1B\,⟹\,B=4.
$$

Thus, the decomposition is

$$
Y(s)=-\frac{2}{s+3}+\frac{4}{s+2}.
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+3}} & ={e}^{-3t} \\ {L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+2}} & ={e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking the inverse Laplace transform of $Y(s),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =-2{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+3}}+4{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+2}} \\ y(t) & =-2{e}^{-3t}+4{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
L{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}=\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4},\,L{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4},
$$

we substitute the known values. Note that $y(0)=-2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(sY(s)-(-2))+3Y(s) & =2(\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4})-3(\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4}) \\ (s+3)Y(s)+2 & =\frac{4-3s}{{s}^{2}+4}\end{aligned}
$$

We rearrange to solve for $Y(s).$ First, subtract $2$ from the right-hand side and find a common denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}(s+3)Y(s) & =\frac{4-3s}{{s}^{2}+4}-2 \\ (s+3)Y(s) & =\frac{4-3s}{{s}^{2}+4}-\frac{2({s}^{2}+4)}{{s}^{2}+4} \\ (s+3)Y(s) & =\frac{-2{s}^{2}-3s-4}{{s}^{2}+4}\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing by $(s+3),$ we obtain

$$
Y(s)=\frac{-2{s}^{2}-3s-4}{(s+3)({s}^{2}+4)}.
$$

Next, we perform a partial fraction decomposition. Since the denominator has a linear factor $(s+3)$ and an irreducible quadratic factor $({s}^{2}+4),$ we write

$$
\frac{-2{s}^{2}-3s-4}{(s+3)({s}^{2}+4)}=\frac{A}{s+3}+\frac{Bs+C}{{s}^{2}+4}.
$$

To find the constants, we clear the denominators:

$$
-2{s}^{2}-3s-4=A({s}^{2}+4)+(Bs+C)(s+3)
$$

- Setting $s=-3,$ we have
 

$$
-2(-3)^{2}-3(-3)-4=A((-3)^{2}+4)+0\,⟹\,-13=13A\,⟹\,A=-1.
$$

- Comparing the coefficients of ${s}^{2},$ we have
  

$$
-2=A+B\,⟹\,-2=-1+B\,⟹\,B=-1.
$$

- Comparing the constant terms, we have
 

$$
-4=4A+3C\,⟹\,-4=4(-1)+3C\,⟹\,C=0.
$$

Thus, the decomposition is

$$
Y(s)=-\frac{1}{s+3}+\frac{-s}{{s}^{2}+4}=-\frac{1}{s+3}-\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4}.
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+3}} & ={e}^{-3t} \\ {L}^{-1}{\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4}} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking the inverse Laplace transform of $Y(s),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =-{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+3}}-{L}^{-1}{\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4}} \\ y(t) & =-{e}^{-3t}-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the following initial value problem.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(0)=2
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below to find the solution using Laplace transforms. You may make use of the following results:

$$
L{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,L{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,s>0.
$$

Let $Y(s)=L{y(t)}.$ Taking the Laplace transform of both sides of the equation and solving for $Y,$ we have

$$
Y(s)={{field-1}}.
$$

The partial fraction decomposition of $Y$ is

$$
Y(s)={{field-2}}.
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(t)={{field-3}}.
$$

First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides of the differential equation. Using the linearity property, we have

$$
L{{y}^{′}}+L{y}=L{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}+L{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}.
$$

Using the formula for the transform of a derivative $L{{y}^{′}}=sY(s)-y(0)$ and the standard trigonometric transforms

$$
L{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}=\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1},\,L{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+1},
$$

we substitute the known values. Note that $y(0)=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(sY(s)-2)+Y(s) & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1}+\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+1} \\ (s+1)Y(s)-2 & =\frac{s+1}{{s}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

We rearrange to solve for $Y(s).$ First, add $2$ to the right-hand side and find a common denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}(s+1)Y(s) & =2+\frac{s+1}{{s}^{2}+1} \\ (s+1)Y(s) & =\frac{2({s}^{2}+1)}{{s}^{2}+1}+\frac{s+1}{{s}^{2}+1} \\ (s+1)Y(s) & =\frac{2{s}^{2}+s+3}{{s}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing by $(s+1),$ we obtain

$$
Y(s)=\frac{2{s}^{2}+s+3}{(s+1)({s}^{2}+1)}.
$$

Next, we perform a partial fraction decomposition. Since the denominator has a linear factor $(s+1)$ and an irreducible quadratic factor $({s}^{2}+1),$ we write

$$
\frac{2{s}^{2}+s+3}{(s+1)({s}^{2}+1)}=\frac{A}{s+1}+\frac{Bs+C}{{s}^{2}+1}.
$$

To find the constants, we clear the denominators:

$$
2{s}^{2}+s+3=A({s}^{2}+1)+(Bs+C)(s+1)
$$

- Setting $s=-1,$ we have
 

$$
2(-1)^{2}+(-1)+3=A((-1)^{2}+1)+0\,⟹\,4=2A\,⟹\,A=2.
$$

- Comparing the coefficients of ${s}^{2},$ we have
  

$$
2=A+B\,⟹\,2=2+B\,⟹\,B=0.
$$

- Comparing the constant terms, we have
 

$$
3=A+C\,⟹\,3=2+C\,⟹\,C=1.
$$

Thus, the decomposition is

$$
Y(s)=\frac{2}{s+1}+\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1}.
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+1}} & ={e}^{-t} \\ {L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1}} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking the inverse Laplace transform of $Y(s),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =2{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+1}}+{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1}} \\ y(t) & =2{e}^{-t}+\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
L{{y}^{′}}+6L{y}=L{\operatorname{sin}⁡3t}+L{\operatorname{cos}⁡3t}.
$$

$$
L{\operatorname{sin}⁡3t}=\frac{3}{{s}^{2}+9},\,L{\operatorname{cos}⁡3t}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+9},
$$

we substitute the known values. Note that $y(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(sY(s)-0)+6Y(s) & =\frac{3}{{s}^{2}+9}+\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+9} \\ (s+6)Y(s) & =\frac{s+3}{{s}^{2}+9}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
Y(s)=\frac{s+3}{(s+6)({s}^{2}+9)}.
$$

$$
\frac{s+3}{(s+6)({s}^{2}+9)}=\frac{A}{s+6}+\frac{Bs+C}{{s}^{2}+9}.
$$

To find the constants, we clear the denominators:

$$
s+3=A({s}^{2}+9)+(Bs+C)(s+6)
$$

- Setting $s=-6,$ we have
 

$$
-6+3=A((-6)^{2}+9)+0\,⟹\,-3=45A\,⟹\,A=-\frac{1}{15}.
$$

- Comparing the coefficients of ${s}^{2},$ we have
  

$$
0=A+B\,⟹\,0=-\frac{1}{15}+B\,⟹\,B=\frac{1}{15}.
$$

- Comparing the constant terms, we have
 

$$
3=9A+6C\,⟹\,3=-\frac{3}{5}+6C\,⟹\,C=\frac{3}{5}.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+6}} & ={e}^{-6t} \\ {L}^{-1}{\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+9}} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡3t \\ {L}^{-1}{\frac{3}{{s}^{2}+9}} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡3t\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

$$
Y(s)={{field-1}}.

$$

$$
y(t)={{field-3}}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides of the differential equation. Using the linearity property, we have

$$
L{{y}^{′}}+2L{y}=L{\operatorname{sin}⁡4t}-L{\operatorname{cos}⁡4t}.
$$

Using the formula for the transform of a derivative $L{{y}^{′}}=sY(s)-y(0)$ and the standard trigonometric transforms

$$
L{\operatorname{sin}⁡4t}=\frac{4}{{s}^{2}+16},\,L{\operatorname{cos}⁡4t}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+16},
$$

we substitute the known values. Note that $y(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(sY(s)-0)+2Y(s) & =\frac{4}{{s}^{2}+16}-\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+16} \\ (s+2)Y(s) & =\frac{4-s}{{s}^{2}+16}\end{aligned}
$$

We rearrange to solve for $Y(s).$ Dividing by $(s+2),$ we obtain

$$
Y(s)=\frac{4-s}{(s+2)({s}^{2}+16)}.
$$

Next, we perform a partial fraction decomposition. Since the denominator has a linear factor $(s+2)$ and an irreducible quadratic factor $({s}^{2}+16),$ we write

$$
\frac{4-s}{(s+2)({s}^{2}+16)}=\frac{A}{s+2}+\frac{Bs+C}{{s}^{2}+16}.
$$

To find the constants, we clear the denominators:

$$
4-s=A({s}^{2}+16)+(Bs+C)(s+2)
$$

- Setting $s=-2,$ we have
 

$$
4-(-2)=A((-2)^{2}+16)+0\,⟹\,6=20A\,⟹\,A=\frac{3}{10}.
$$

- Comparing the coefficients of ${s}^{2},$ we have
  

$$
0=A+B\,⟹\,0=\frac{3}{10}+B\,⟹\,B=-\frac{3}{10}.
$$

- Comparing the constant terms, we have
 

$$
4=16A+2C\,⟹\,4=\frac{48}{10}+2C\,⟹\,C=-\frac{2}{5}.
$$

Thus, the decomposition is

$$
Y(s)=\frac{3}{10(s+2)}+\frac{(-\frac{3}{10}s-\frac{2}{5})}{{s}^{2}+16}=\frac{3}{10(s+2)}-\frac{3s+4}{10({s}^{2}+16)}.
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+2}} & ={e}^{-2t} \\ {L}^{-1}{\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+16}} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡4t \\ {L}^{-1}{\frac{4}{{s}^{2}+16}} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking the inverse Laplace transform of $Y(s),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =\frac{3}{10}{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+2}}-\frac{3}{10}{L}^{-1}{\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+16}}-\frac{1}{10}{L}^{-1}{\frac{4}{{s}^{2}+16}} \\ y(t) & =\frac{3}{10}{e}^{-2t}-\frac{3}{10}\operatorname{cos}⁡4t-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡4t.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the Laplace transform $Y(s) = \mathcal L\{y(t)\}$ for $s > 1$ if 

$$
y' + y =  2e^t, \qquad y(0)=-1.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the addition and scalar multiplication properties of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{′}+y} & =L{2{e}^{t}} \\ L{{y}^{′}}+L{y} & =2L{{e}^{t}}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate $\mathcal L\left\{ y' \right\},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of a derivative and the initial condition $y(0)=-1\mathbin{:}$

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{y'\right\}  = sY(s) - y(0)   = sY(s) + 1
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms:

$$
\mathcal L \{e^{at}\} = \dfrac{1}{s-a}, \qquad s > a
$$

Therefore, we have the following result:

$$
\mathcal{L} \{ e^t \}  = \dfrac{1}{s-1}
$$

Therefore, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{′}}+L{y} & =2L{{e}^{t}} \\ (sY(s)+1)+Y(s) & =\frac{2}{s-1} \\ (s+1)Y(s) & =\frac{2}{s-1}-1 \\ (s+1)Y(s) & =\frac{2-(s-1)}{s-1} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{3-s}{{s}^{2}-1}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below to find the solution using Laplace transforms.

Let $Y(s) = \mathcal L \{y(t)\}.$ Taking the Laplace transform of both sides of the equation and solving for $Y,$ we have

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14072504/assets/1da481c39504266a4f42e13ef938ff0f7eb75d1174a149bed8d80e47e25d46e6.png)

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides of the differential equation. Using the linearity property, we have

$$
\mathcal{L}\{y'\} + 4\mathcal{L}\{y\} = 3\mathcal{L}\{e^{-t}\}.
$$

Using the formula for the transform of a derivative, $\mathcal{L}\{y'\} = sY(s) - y(0),$ and the standard transform 

$$
\mathcal{L}\{e^{at}\} = \frac{1}{s-a}, \qquad s > a,
$$

we substitute the known values. Note that $y(0)=2{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}(sY(s)-2)+4Y(s) & =3\cdot \frac{1}{s+1} \\ (s+4)Y(s)-2 & =\frac{3}{s+1}\end{aligned}
$$

We rearrange to solve for $Y(s).$ First, add $2$ to the right-hand side and find a common denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}(s+4)Y(s) & =2+\frac{3}{s+1} \\ (s+4)Y(s) & =\frac{2(s+1)}{s+1}+\frac{3}{s+1} \\ (s+4)Y(s) & =\frac{2s+5}{s+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing by $(s+4),$ we obtain

$$
Y(s) =\dfrac{2s+5}{(s + 4)(s+1)}.
$$

Next, we perform a partial fraction decomposition. We write $Y(s)$ in the form

$$
\dfrac{2s+5}{(s+4)(s+1)} = \dfrac{A}{s+4} + \dfrac{B}{s+1}.
$$

To find the constants $A$ and $B,$ we first clear the denominators:

$$
2s+5 = A(s+1) + B(s+4)
$$

Now, we find the constants $A$ and $B.$

- Setting $s = -4,$ we have

$$
2(-4)+5 = A(-4+1) + B(0) \implies -3 = -3A \implies A = 1.
$$

- Setting $s = -1,$ we have

$$
2(-1)+5 = A(0) + B(-1+4) \implies 3 = 3B \implies B = 1.
$$

Thus, the decomposition is

$$
Y(s) = \dfrac{1}{s+4} + \dfrac{1}{s+1}.
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+4}} & ={e}^{-4t} \\ {L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+1}} & ={e}^{-t}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking the inverse Laplace transform of $Y(s),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+4}}+{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+1}} \\ y(t) & ={e}^{-4t}+{e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula for the transform of a derivative $\mathcal{L}\{y'\} = sY(s) - y(0)$ and the standard trigonometric transform

$$
\mathcal{L}\{\sin t\} = \dfrac{1}{s^2+1},
$$

we substitute the known values. Note that $y(0)=1{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}(sY(s)-1)-2Y(s) & =-5\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1} \\ (s-2)Y(s)-1 & =-\frac{5}{{s}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

We rearrange to solve for $Y(s).$ First, add $1$ to the right-hand side and find a common denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}(s-2)Y(s) & =1-\frac{5}{{s}^{2}+1} \\ (s-2)Y(s) & =\frac{{s}^{2}+1}{{s}^{2}+1}-\frac{5}{{s}^{2}+1} \\ (s-2)Y(s) & =\frac{{s}^{2}-4}{{s}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing by $(s-2),$ we obtain

$$
Y(s) =\dfrac{s^2 - 4}{(s - 2)(s^2 + 1)} = \dfrac{(s-2)(s+2)}{(s - 2)(s^2 + 1)} = \dfrac{s+2}{s^2 + 1}.
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+1}} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ {L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1}} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking the inverse Laplace transform of $Y(s),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+1}}+2{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1}} \\ y(t) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$
